conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Claire, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers in the weeks and months after birth, and I’m really glad you’re here.

In front of us we have the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a short questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically since your baby arrived. We use it with every new parent because mood changes are very common after childbirth, and we want to be sure you have the support you need.

Everything we talk about stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. We’ll simply go through ten questions about the past seven days; each one just takes a moment. If anything feels difficult or confusing, we can pause or talk it through.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[quiet half-shrug, eyes a little glassy]

Honestly… most of the time it feels hard. My husband tried showing me a silly video the other night and I just… couldn’t muster a real laugh. I managed a polite smile because I didn’t want him to worry, but nothing feels funny lately. I’d say I haven’t really laughed in the past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No… not really. I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed. Sometimes I pretend to smile so people don’t worry, but nothing feels funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[looks down at hands]

Not much… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels like another chore. I’m going through the motions, but there’s no real “looking forward” feeling.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[voice drops, fingers twisting the hem of my sweater]

Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking, “I’m doing something wrong, I’m a terrible mom.” I know rationally he’s just a baby, but the guilt still hits—like every hiccup is my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[lets out a shaky breath]

All the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing—even though he’s right there, perfectly fine. Or I’ll lie awake picturing him rolling off the changing table, even though I’m always holding the strap. It’s like my mind won’t stop catastrophizing, and I can’t switch it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands, voice tight]

Yes… a few nights this week I’ve woken up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, sure something awful is about to happen. There’s no real reason—baby’s asleep, the house is quiet—but I feel like I can’t catch my breath. It passes after a while, but in the moment it’s terrifying.
Things have been getting on top of me

[eyes well up]

Yeah… most days. It feels like the second I finish one feed, there’s another, or the laundry’s piled up again, or I haven’t eaten a real meal in two days. I keep thinking, “How does everyone else manage?” I’m not falling apart, but it’s like I’m treading water and my legs are getting tired.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[nods slowly, voice barely above a whisper]

Yes… even when the baby finally settles, I lie there staring at the ceiling. My mind just keeps spinning—worries about tomorrow, guilt about today, replaying every little thing I did wrong. Some nights I drift off around three, then I hear him stir and I’m wide-awake again.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes fixed on the floor]

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be rocking the baby and tears just start rolling—no real trigger, just this aching sadness I can’t shake. I keep waiting for it to pass, but it sticks around.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[presses lips together, nods]

Yes… I’ve cried three, maybe four times this week. Once was after a phone call when Grandma asked how I was doing—I said “fine,” hung up, and burst into tears. Another time the baby wouldn’t latch and I just sobbed while my partner held us both. It feels like the tears are right under the surface all the time.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I’ve felt low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting concerns endorsed across 10-item review:  
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent dysphoria with daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep disruption linked to rumination/guilt (Q7)  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Unprompted anxiety, catastrophic worry, nocturnal panic (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and inadequate coping (Q6)  

Safety: Denies self-harm ideation (Q10). No protective concerns voiced.

Risk factors: Primiparous status, loss of pleasure, prominent guilt, anxiety with panic equivalents, and functional impairment (feeding, sleep).

Screening significance: High endorsement pattern consistent with probable major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; further diagnostic evaluation and safety planning recommended.
